title: Abbreviated Syllabus
text:
Understanding statistics is vitally important for work in Psychology. Data analytic techniques form the bedrock for many avenues of scientific research, and understanding their theory implies knowing when a particular approach is appropriate and, more critically, when it is not.
In Introduction to Data Analysis in Psychology, students gain a foundation for conducting research, interpreting results, and understanding more complex statistical models used in psychology.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Week 2 develops the first major set of descriptive-statistical tools for organizing psychological data. The central question is simple:

Once data have been collected, how should we represent them so that their structure can be understood accurately?

The week begins by reviewing summation notation and then turns to types of variables, scales of measurement, frequency distributions, grouped and ungrouped data, and graphical displays. The assigned readings also introduce central tendency—the mean, median, and mode—as another way to summarize a distribution with a single representative value.
The lecture emphasizes that numerical codes do not automatically determine what mathematical operations are meaningful. The appropriate analysis depends on what the variable actually represents (Sigal, 2026). Privitera (2018, 2024) develops the same general principle through scales of measurement, frequency distributions, and central tendency.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you should be able to:

Distinguish categorical/discrete variables from continuous/quantitative variables.
Define and recognize the four scales of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio.
Explain what information is—and is not—contained in each scale of measurement.
Explain why numerical coding does not necessarily make a variable quantitative.
Construct an ungrouped frequency distribution.
Calculate frequency, proportion/relative frequency, percentage, cumulative frequency, and cumulative relative frequency/percentage.
Explain when grouped frequency distributions are useful.
Calculate a reasonable class interval/bin width, and identify lower and upper limits.
Distinguish apparent limits from real limits.
Choose an appropriate graph for a variable: bar chart, histogram, or frequency polygon.
Explain how graphical design choices can create misleading impressions.
Use summation notation correctly when constants, products, and multiple variables are involved.
Define mean, median, and mode and explain how the appropriate measure of central tendency depends on the data and distribution.
Identify a documented disagreement in the Week 2 materials concerning how Likert-like/rating-scale data should be treated.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Frequency
Frequency (f) is the number of observations at a value or in an interval.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Proportion / relative frequency
\[
p=\frac{f}{n}.
\]
The proportions should sum to approximately:
\[
\sum p=1.00.
\]

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Percentage
\[
\%=p\times100.
\]
Percentages should sum to approximately:
\[
100\%.
\]

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Cumulative frequency
Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies.
For an ascending table, it answers:

How many observations scored this value or less?

The final cumulative frequency should equal (n).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Cumulative relative frequency / cumulative percentage
A cumulative relative frequency is the running total of proportions.
A cumulative percentage is the running total of percentages.
The final values should be approximately:
\[
1.00
\]
and
\[
100\%.
\]
respectively (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Measurement Scales

Preferred web browser: nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio?
Finishing position in a marathon: nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio?
Celsius temperature: nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio?
Reaction time in milliseconds: nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio?
Explain why coding categories 1, 2, 3, and 4 does not automatically justify calculating their mean.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Frequency Tables
For:
\[
X=\{2,4,4,5,5,5,7,8,8,9\},
\]
construct a table containing:

(X);
(f);
(p);
percentage;
cumulative frequency;
cumulative percentage.

Check that:
\[
\sum f=n,
\]
\[
\sum p=1,
\]
and percentages sum to 100%.

title: Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:
Grouping
For scores ranging from 12 to 92:

Calculate the observed range.
Estimate a bin width for approximately 10 bins.
Propose a set of non-overlapping class intervals.
Explain what information is lost after grouping.

Week 02 — Data Types, Frequency Distributions, and Visualization
text:

For:
\[
2,3,4,5,6,6,100
\]
calculate:

mean;
median;
mode.

Then explain which value is most representative and why.

title: Data Analysis: Learning & Teaching
text:
This repository supports learning and teaching introductory data analysis in psychology. It is designed as a structured resource for reviewing statistical concepts, preparing tutorials, and connecting lectures, readings, exercises, and assignments.
The course emphasizes conceptual understanding: not simply how to perform a statistical procedure, but how to recognize when a method is appropriate, what assumptions it makes, and how results should be interpreted.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Week 1 introduces the logic of data analysis in psychology. The central idea is that statistics is not simply a collection of formulas. It is a way to connect questions, theories, measurements, data, and evidence-based conclusions.
The lecture begins with the goals of science and then moves through the basic research process: identify something that needs explaining, decide how to measure it, formulate a research hypothesis, collect data, and analyze those data descriptively or inferentially. It also introduces the distinction between populations and samples, basic research designs, and several mathematical tools—especially summation notation—that will be used throughout the course.
The tutorials and practice materials reinforce these ideas through hands-on work with summation notation and the basic organization of data into frequency tables and histograms.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Week 1 introduces the logic of data analysis in psychology. The central idea is that statistics is not simply a collection of formulas. It is a way to connect questions, theories, measurements, data, and evidence-based conclusions.
The lecture begins with the goals of science and then moves through the basic research process: identify something that needs explaining, decide how to measure it, formulate a research hypothesis, collect data, and analyze those data descriptively or inferentially. It also introduces the distinction between populations and samples, basic research designs, and several mathematical tools—especially summation notation—that will be used throughout the course.
The tutorials and practice materials reinforce these ideas through hands-on work with summation notation and the basic organization of data into frequency tables and histograms.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you should be able to:

Explain why statistics is important for psychological research.
Distinguish descriptive statistics from inferential statistics.
Distinguish a population from a sample, and a parameter from a statistic.
Explain what a variable is and distinguish independent, dependent, and extraneous/confounding variables.
Explain the difference between a research hypothesis and a statistical hypothesis.
Distinguish experimental, quasi-experimental, and correlational/observational research designs.
Explain why representativeness and sampling error matter when generalizing from a sample to a population.
Use basic mathematical notation correctly, including order of operations, exponents, roots, inequalities, and summation notation.
Read and construct basic frequency tables using frequency, proportion, percentage, cumulative frequency, and cumulative relative frequency.
Explain what a histogram shows and how grouped and ungrouped histograms summarize distributions.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Operational definitions
Psychological concepts are often abstract. Anxiety, memory, stress, motivation, intelligence, and attention are not directly visible in the same way as height or weight.
Researchers therefore need to operationally define variables.
An operational definition states exactly how a concept will be observed or measured.
For example:

“anxiety” might be measured using a questionnaire score;
“memory” might be measured as the number of words correctly recalled;
“autonomic arousal” might be measured using heart rate or blood pressure.

Operational definitions connect theoretical ideas to observable data.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Descriptive statistics
Descriptive statistics summarize and organize data.
They answer questions such as:

What values occurred?
How frequently did they occur?
What is a typical score?
How spread out are the scores?
What does the distribution look like?

Descriptive statistics can be presented as numbers, tables, graphs, percentages, frequencies, and averages.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Inferential statistics
Inferential statistics use data from a sample to make a reasoned statement about a larger population.
The logic is:
Population → Sample → Data → Statistical analysis → Inference about the population
This is a conceptual leap because researchers usually observe only the sample, while their scientific question concerns the larger population.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Experimental design
A true experiment is designed to support a cause-and-effect conclusion.
The lecture emphasizes three important features:

Manipulation — the researcher creates different conditions.
Randomization — participants are randomly allocated to conditions.
Comparison/control — outcomes are compared across conditions.


Example
To study whether watching television affects reaction time:

participants could be randomly assigned to a TV condition or a no-TV condition;
the researcher manipulates whether television is present;
reaction time is measured in both groups.

Random assignment is important because it helps distribute other participant characteristics across conditions.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Quasi-experimental design
A quasi-experiment resembles an experiment but lacks one or more elements needed for a true experiment.
This often happens because:

the independent variable cannot be manipulated;
participants cannot be randomly assigned;
a comparison/control group is missing.

Many psychological variables are preexisting and cannot ethically or practically be randomized.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Correlational or observational design
In a correlational design, researchers measure two or more variables without manipulating them.
The purpose is to determine whether variables are related.
For example:

computer use and exercise;
extroversion and school achievement;
income and life satisfaction.

A correlational design can demonstrate a relationship, but it cannot by itself establish causation.

Comparison

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Order of operations
Use PEDMAS/BEDMAS:

Parentheses / Brackets
Exponents
Division / Multiplication
Addition / Subtraction

Changing the order can produce completely different results.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Brackets and absolute value
Parentheses and square brackets group operations.
Absolute-value brackets indicate distance from zero:
\[
|4| = 4
\]
\[
|-39| = 39
\]

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Inequalities
Know the meaning of \(>\), \(<\), and \(\leq\).

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Fractions
You should be able to add and subtract fractions, find common denominators, and convert fractions to decimals.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Negative numbers
\[
(-a)(b) = -ab
\]
\[
(-a)(-b) = ab
\]

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Basic equations
For example:
\[
15x + 10 = 40
\]
Subtract 10 from both sides:
\[
15x = 30
\]
Then divide by 15:
\[
x = 2
\]

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Exponents and square roots
\[
3^2 = 9
\]
\[
\sqrt{9} = 3
\]
\[
3^4 = 81
\]

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Indices matter
If
\[
X = \{4,8,6,3,5,6,4,2\}
\]
then
\[
\sum_{i=2}^{5} X_i = 8 + 6 + 3 + 5 = 22
\]
Only values with indices 2 through 5 are included.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Summing products
If two variables are paired,
\[
\sum XY
\]
means multiply \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) within each row and then add the resulting products.
It does not mean
\[
(\sum X)(\sum Y)
\]
unless that is explicitly written.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
section: Squaring a sum is not the same as summing squares
text:
Squaring a sum is not the same as summing squares
These expressions are different:
\[
\left(\sum X\right)^2
\]
and
\[
\sum X^2
\]
For example, if \(X=\{1,2,3\}\):
\[
\left(\sum X\right)^2 = (1+2+3)^2 = 36
\]
but
\[
\sum X^2 = 1^2+2^2+3^2 = 14
\]
This distinction becomes extremely important later in formulas for variance and other statistics.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Parentheses prevent ambiguity
Compare:
\[
\sum(X_i + 2)
\]
with
\[
\left(\sum X_i\right)+2
\]
They are not equivalent.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Frequency
The frequency \(f\) is the number of observations with a particular value.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Proportion / relative frequency
\[
\text{Proportion}=\frac{f}{n}
\]

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Percentage frequency
\[
\text{Percentage}= \frac{f}{n}\times 100
\]

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Cumulative frequency
Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies as scores increase. The final cumulative frequency should equal \(n\).

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Cumulative relative frequency
This is the running total of proportions. The final value should equal 1.00.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Cumulative percentage
The final cumulative percentage should equal 100%.

Internal checks
A correctly completed frequency table should satisfy:
\[
\sum f=n
\]
\[
\sum \text{Prop.}=1.00
\]
\[
\sum \%=100\%
\]
and the last cumulative entries should be \(CF=n\), \(CRF=1.00\), and \(C\%=100\%\).

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
“Statistics proves that something is true.”
No. Statistical analysis helps quantify evidence and uncertainty. Conclusions remain dependent on the study design, measurement quality, sample, assumptions, and context.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
section: “A sample is basically the same thing as a population.”
text:
“A sample is basically the same thing as a population.”
No. A sample is only a subset. Inferential statistics is needed precisely because we usually do not observe the whole population.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
section: “A statistic and a parameter are interchangeable.”
text:
“A statistic and a parameter are interchangeable.”
No. Statistic → sample; parameter → population.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
section: “Random assignment and random sampling are the same.”
text:
“Random assignment and random sampling are the same.”
No. Random sampling concerns how people are selected from a population. Random assignment concerns how selected participants are placed into experimental conditions.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
section: “Correlation shows that one variable causes the other.”
text:
“Correlation shows that one variable causes the other.”
No. Correlation shows a relationship, not cause.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
section: “\(\sum X^2\) and \((\sum X)^2\) mean the same thing.”
text:
“\(\sum X^2\) and \((\sum X)^2\) mean the same thing.”
No. One squares each score before summing; the other sums first and then squares.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
section: “The number after sigma is always added once.”
text:
“The number after sigma is always added once.”
Not necessarily. If a constant is inside the summation, it is applied once for each indexed observation.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
section: “A histogram is an objective picture of the data.”
text:
“A histogram is an objective picture of the data.”
The data are objective observations, but the display still depends on choices such as bin width, axis range, and grouping.

title: Week 01 — Course Introduction and Basic Concepts
text:
Conceptual questions students may ask

“Why do we need statistics if we can just look at the data?”
Raw data often contain too many individual observations to interpret easily. Descriptive statistics organize the observations; inferential statistics help researchers reason beyond the observed sample.


“Why can experiments show causation but correlations cannot?”
A properly conducted experiment uses manipulation, random assignment, and comparison/control. These design features help rule out competing explanations. A correlation only observes how variables co-vary.


“Why do we care so much about populations if we only collect samples?”
Psychological research usually aims to understand a broader group or process, not only the particular participants who happened to take part.


“Why is summation notation necessary?”
Statistical formulas often apply the same arithmetic operation to many observations. Summation notation provides a compact and precise way to express this.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
section: 1. Why Do We Need Measures of Center?
text:
1. Why Do We Need Measures of Center?
A frequency distribution tells us how scores are distributed, but researchers often also want a single value that summarizes what is typical or representative.
The Week 3 lecture frames central tendency as an attempt to locate the “center” of a sample or population, while emphasizing that “center” can mean different things (Sigal, 2026).
The three standard measures are:

Mode
Median
Mean

Each defines “center” differently.



Measure
Basic idea




Mode
Most frequently occurring value/category


Median
Middle position in terms of frequency


Mean
Arithmetic balance point in terms of magnitudes



The fact that there are three measures is not redundancy. They behave differently and are useful under different conditions.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
2. The Mode
The mode is the value or category that occurs most often.
For:
\[
X=\{0,1,2,2,3\},
\]
the mode is:
\[
2.
\]
The lecture recommends a simple procedure:

inspect the values;
sort if useful;
count frequencies;
identify the value with the highest frequency (Sigal, 2026).


More than one mode
For:
\[
X=\{0,1,1,1,1,2,2,3,3,3,3,5\},
\]
both 1 and 3 occur four times.
The distribution is therefore bimodal.
A distribution may be:

unimodal — one mode;
bimodal — two modes;
multimodal — more than two modes;
nonmodal — no value occurs more often than the others.



Why the mode is special
The mode can be used with categorical data because it depends only on frequency.
For example, if browser preference is categorical, the “most common browser” is meaningful even though an arithmetic mean of browser codes would not be.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
3. The Median
The median is the value that divides an ordered distribution in half based on frequency.
It is also the 50th percentile (Sigal, 2026).
The median is not necessarily an observed score.

Basic position rule
A common quick rule for the median position is:
\[
\frac{n+1}{2}.
\]
For an odd sample size:
\[
X=\{11,5,8,10,3\}.
\]
Sort the values:
\[
\{3,5,8,10,11\}.
\]
Because:
\[
\frac{5+1}{2}=3,
\]
the median is the third score:
\[
Md=8.
\]

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
section: 4. Median With an Even Number of Scores
text:
4. Median With an Even Number of Scores
Suppose:
\[
X=\{3,3,4,5,7,8\}.
\]
Then:
\[
\frac{6+1}{2}=3.5.
\]
The median falls halfway between positions 3 and 4.
Average those two scores:
\[
Md=\frac{4+5}{2}=4.5.
\]
For ordinary ungrouped data, this is the familiar textbook procedure.
However, the Week 3 lecture introduces a more general interpolation method because the instructor wants students to think about the median as a location within an interval, especially when ties or grouped data are involved (Sigal, 2026).

text:
7. A Course-Specific Median Convention
There is an important methodological point here.
For simple ungrouped raw data, many statistics texts define the median as the middle observed score, or the average of the two middle observed scores when (n) is even. The Week 3 lecture deliberately goes beyond that quick rule and uses interpolation based on cumulative frequency—even when scores are tied—because the instructor wants students to conceptualize percentiles as positions within score intervals (Sigal, 2026).
The supplemental median handout makes this intention explicit. It states that the quick ((n+1)/2) rule can be misleading for binned data with many ties and demonstrates a grouped age example in which the median is estimated as 24.1 rather than simply reporting the category 24–26 (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026a).

For this course
When solving course problems that ask for the formula-based median:

Use the interpolation procedure demonstrated in the lecture and supplemental handout.

Do not silently substitute the simpler textbook convention when the problem is clearly designed around cumulative frequency and real limits.

text:
8. Percentiles Beyond the Median
The (0.5) in the median formula is not arbitrary.
It represents the desired percentile:
\[
P_{50}.
\]
The same logic can be generalized.
For example, the 25th percentile can be estimated using:
\[
P_{25}
=
LL+
W\left[
\frac{0.25n-cf}{f}
\right].
\]
Thus the median formula is part of a more general percentile-interpolation framework (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
11. The Mean
The mean is the arithmetic average.
For a sample:
\[
\bar{x}
=
\frac{\sum x_i}{n}.
\]
The lecture notes that APA-style reporting commonly uses (M) for a sample mean, while () is used for a population mean (Sigal, 2026).
For:
\[
X=\{3,7,4,6\},
\]
\[
\bar{x}
=
\frac{3+7+4+6}{4}
=
\frac{20}{4}
=
5.
\]
Conceptually, the mean is a balance point based on magnitudes.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
12. Sample and Population Mean Notation
The lecture distinguishes:

sample mean: ({x}) or (M);
population mean: ().

The calculation itself is structurally the same:
\[
M=\frac{\sum X}{n},
\]
and:
\[
\mu=\frac{\sum X}{N}.
\]
The symbols remind us whether the calculation describes a sample or the entire population of interest.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
13. The Weighted Mean
A simple average of group means is only correct when the groups contribute equal weight.
Suppose:

Group 1: ({x}_1=6, n_1=20)
Group 2: ({x}_2=15, n_2=3)

It would be wrong to calculate:
\[
\frac{6+15}{2}=10.5.
\]
The groups are not equally large.
Instead:
\[
\bar{x}_C
=
\frac{\sum X_1+\sum X_2}
{n_1+n_2}.
\]
Because:
\[
\sum X_1=120
\]
and:
\[
\sum X_2=45,
\]
the combined mean is:
\[
\bar{x}_C
=
\frac{120+45}{20+3}
=
\frac{165}{23}
=
7.17.
\]
The larger group contributes more information and therefore more weight (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
14. Weighted Mean From Group Means
If the original sums are not given, recover each group sum using:
\[
\sum X = \bar{x}n.
\]
Then:
\[
\bar{x}_C
=
\frac{
\bar{x}_1n_1+\bar{x}_2n_2+\cdots+\bar{x}_kn_k
}{
n_1+n_2+\cdots+n_k
}.
\]
The lecture example gives:

\[

=

{7+20+45}
=
\frac{262}{72}
=

\]

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
15. How the Mean Changes
The Week 3 worksheet asks students to explore how transformations affect the mean (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026b).
The key patterns are:

Change one score
Changing one observation changes the mean because the total sum changes.


Add a constant to every score
If every observation increases by (c),
\[
M_{\text{new}}=M_{\text{old}}+c.
\]


Multiply every score by a constant
If every observation is multiplied by (c),
\[
M_{\text{new}}=cM_{\text{old}}.
\]


Subtract the mean from every score
If:
\[
Y_i=X_i-M,
\]
then:
\[
\bar{Y}=0.
\]
This is because deviations from the mean sum to zero.


Add a new score
A new score above the old mean pulls the mean upward.
A new score below the old mean pulls the mean downward.
A new score equal to the old mean leaves the mean unchanged.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
section: 16. Why Do We Need Three Measures of Center?
text:
16. Why Do We Need Three Measures of Center?
The lecture answers this by asking what kinds of data and distributions we have (Sigal, 2026).

Mode
Useful for:

categorical/discrete data;
identifying the most common response;
describing modality.



Median
Useful when:

scores are ordinal;
the distribution has extreme scores or outliers;
a robust description of the middle is desirable.



Mean
Useful in many quantitative settings because it incorporates the magnitude of every score.
The key principle is:

The best measure depends on the structure of the data.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
17. Outliers: Mean vs. Median
The lecture gives the following error counts:



Errors
0
1
2
3
100




Frequency
1
4
3
1
1



The raw scores are:
\[
0,1,1,1,1,2,2,2,3,100.
\]
The mean is:
\[
M
=
\frac{113}{10}
=
11.3.
\]
This is a poor description of the typical observation because one extreme score pulls the mean upward.
Using the course’s interpolated median method, the lecture obtains:
\[
Md=1.5.
\]
The example demonstrates why the median can be more robust to extreme values than the mean (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
19. Mean, Median, Mode, and Shape
The lecture presents a useful heuristic:

Approximately symmetric / bell-shaped
\[
\text{mean} \approx \text{median} \approx \text{mode}.
\]


Positive skew
\[
\text{mean}>\text{median}>\text{mode}.
\]


Negative skew
\[
\text{mean}<\text{median}<\text{mode}.
\]
The reason is that the mean is particularly sensitive to extreme values and is pulled toward the long tail (Sigal, 2026).
These relationships are useful descriptive clues, not universal mathematical identities for every irregular dataset.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
22. The Range
The range is:
\[
\text{Range}
=
X_{\max}-X_{\min}.
\]
It is the simplest measure of variability.
For:
\[
1,2,3,4,5,
\]
\[
\text{Range}=5-1=4.
\]

Limitation
The range uses only two observations:

the minimum;
the maximum.

Therefore, a single extreme score can drastically inflate it.
Privitera (2018, 2024) emphasizes that the range is most informative when important outliers are absent.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
23. Interquartile Range
The interquartile range (IQR) describes the spread of the middle 50% of a distribution.
It is:
\[
IQR=Q_3-Q_1.
\]
where:

(Q_1) = 25th percentile;
(Q_2) = median / 50th percentile;
(Q_3) = 75th percentile.

Because the top and bottom 25% are excluded, the IQR is less sensitive to extreme scores than the full range (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
24. From Deviation to Variance
Suppose we want to quantify how far scores are from the mean.
For each score:
\[
\text{deviation}
=
X_i-M.
\]
If the data are:
\[
X=\{3,4,5,6,12\},
\]
the mean is:
\[
M=6.
\]
The deviations are:
\[
-3,-2,-1,0,6.
\]
But:
\[
\sum(X_i-M)=0.
\]
Positive and negative deviations cancel.
Therefore, simply averaging raw signed deviations would always make variability look like zero.
This is why deviations are squared before they are summed.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
25. Sum of Squares
The sum of squares (SS) is:
\[
SS
=
\sum(X_i-M)^2
\]
for a sample, or:
\[
SS
=
\sum(X_i-\mu)^2
\]
for a population.
Because each deviation is squared:

negative signs disappear;
larger deviations contribute more;
(SS).

If every observation is identical, every deviation is zero, and:
\[
SS=0.
\]
Privitera (2018, 2024) describes SS as the sum of squared deviations from the mean and the numerator used in the variance formulas.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
26. Population Variance
Population variance is:
\[
\sigma^2
=
\frac{
\sum(X_i-\mu)^2
}{N}
=
\frac{SS}{N}.
\]
The lecture example uses:
\[
X=\{1,0,6,1\}
\]
with:
\[
\mu=2.
\]
The deviations are:
\[
-1,-2,4,-1.
\]
Squared deviations:
\[
1,4,16,1.
\]
Thus:
\[
SS=22.
\]
Population variance is:
\[
\sigma^2
=
\frac{22}{4}
=
5.5.
\]

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
27. Standard Deviation for a Population
The population standard deviation is the square root of the population variance:
\[
\sigma
=
\sqrt{\sigma^2}.
\]
For the previous example:
\[
\sigma
=
\sqrt{5.5}
\approx
2.35.
\]
Variance is expressed in squared units.
Standard deviation returns the measure of spread to the original units of measurement (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
28. Sample Variance
When the observed data are a sample rather than the entire population, the Week 3 materials use:
\[
s^2
=
\frac{
\sum(X_i-\bar{X})^2
}{n-1}
=
\frac{SS}{n-1}.
\]
Using the same values:
\[
X=\{1,0,6,1\},
\]
we still have:
\[
SS=22.
\]
But now:
\[
s^2
=
\frac{22}{4-1}
=
\frac{22}{3}
\approx
7.33.
\]
The sample standard deviation is:
\[
s
=
\sqrt{7.33}
\approx
2.71.
\]

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
29. Why Does Sample Variance Use (n-1)?
This is one of the most important conceptual ideas in Week 3.
If we calculate sample variance using (n), it tends to underestimate the population variance.
Dividing by:
\[
n-1
\]
makes the sample variance a better estimator of population variance on average (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).
Privitera describes this as an unbiased estimator:

Across repeated random samples, variance calculated with (n-1) equals the population variance on average.

This correction is often associated with Bessel’s correction.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
30. Degrees of Freedom
The denominator:
\[
n-1
\]
is also the degrees of freedom for sample variance.
Degrees of freedom can be understood as the number of scores that remain free to vary once the sample mean is known.
Suppose a sample contains three scores and has:
\[
M=4.
\]
If two scores are:
\[
3,\ 4,
\]
then the third cannot be arbitrary.
Because the three scores must sum to:
\[
3(4)=12,
\]
the missing value must be:
\[
5.
\]
Thus only:
\[
n-1
\]
scores are independently free to vary (Privitera, 2018, 2024; Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
31. Standard Deviation
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance.
For a sample:
\[
s=\sqrt{s^2}
=
\sqrt{\frac{SS}{n-1}}.
\]
For a population:
\[
\sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}
=
\sqrt{\frac{SS}{N}}.
\]
The standard deviation gives a measure of the typical distance of scores from the mean in the original scale of measurement (Privitera, 2018, 2024).

Interpretation

smaller SD → scores are more tightly clustered around the mean;
larger SD → scores are more widely spread.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
32. Variance vs. Standard Deviation



Quantity
What it measures
Units




Variance
Average squared spread from the mean
Squared units


Standard deviation
Spread around the mean
Original units



For example, if heights are measured in inches:

variance is in inches squared;
standard deviation is in inches.

This is one reason standard deviation is easier to interpret directly.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
section: 33. What Happens When Scores Are Transformed?
text:
33. What Happens When Scores Are Transformed?
The Week 3 worksheet explicitly asks students to investigate transformations (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026b).

Add or subtract the same constant from every score
If:
\[
Y_i=X_i+c,
\]
then the mean shifts:
\[
M_Y=M_X+c.
\]
But distances from the mean do not change.
Therefore:
\[
s_Y=s_X
\]
and:
\[
s_Y^2=s_X^2.
\]


Multiply every score by a constant
If:
\[
Y_i=cX_i,
\]
then:
\[
M_Y=cM_X,
\]
\[
s_Y=|c|s_X,
\]
and:
\[
s_Y^2=c^2s_X^2.
\]
These relationships are central to understanding standardization later in the course.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
35. A Second Worksheet Dataset
The worksheet also gives weekly grocery-shopping times:
\[
75,72,71,55,56,72,93,73,72,72,73,91,66,71,56,59.
\]
Students are asked to calculate:

mode;
median;
mean;
range;
standard deviation (PSYC 210 Teaching Team, 2026b).

This problem integrates central tendency and variability into one descriptive summary.
That is the larger Week 3 goal:

A useful description of a dataset normally requires more than one statistic.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
36. What Should Be Reported Together?
Measures of center and variability are most informative when interpreted together.
For many quantitative variables, researchers commonly report:
\[
M\pm SD.
\]
The mean tells us about the center.
The standard deviation tells us about spread around that center.
Privitera (2018, 2024) emphasizes that the standard deviation is especially informative when reported with the mean.
For skewed distributions or variables with important outliers, a median paired with a robust measure such as the IQR may be more informative.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
37. Choosing Measures for Lucy’s Dataset
The lecture returns to Lucy’s dataset:








Variable
Type
Potential useful summary




Name
Identifier
None as a quantitative summary


Age
Quantitative
Mean/median + SD/range


IQ
Quantitative
Mean + SD; inspect shape/outliers


Height
Quantitative
Mean + SD


Grade

Median/mode; frequencies


Browser
Nominal
Mode; frequencies


CARS

Mean/median + variability, depending on distribution and course assumptions



The point is not that one fixed rule always applies.
The choice depends on:

scale of measurement;
distribution shape;
outliers;
the substantive research question (Sigal, 2026).

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
38. How the Concepts Fit Together
Week 3 can be understood as a sequence:
What is the distribution’s center?
↓
Mode, median, mean
↓
What is the distribution’s shape?
↓
Symmetric? Positively skewed? Negatively skewed? Multimodal?
↓
How spread out are the observations?
↓
Range, IQR, variance, standard deviation
↓
Sample or population?
↓
Use (N) or (n-1)
↓
Interpret center and spread together
This is the transition from simply organizing data to describing the mathematical structure of a distribution.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
39. Important Terms







Term
Plain-language explanation




Mode
Most frequently occurring value or category.


Median
Middle position of an ordered distribution; 50th percentile.


Mean
Arithmetic average; balance point based on magnitudes.


Weighted mean
Mean in which groups/values contribute according to their weights or sample sizes.


Skewness
Asymmetry of a distribution.


Positive skew
Long tail toward larger values.


Negative skew
Long tail toward smaller values.


Variability
Degree to which scores are dispersed or spread.


Range
Maximum minus minimum.


Quartile
Boundary dividing a distribution into four parts.


Interquartile range (IQR)
(Q_3-Q_1); spread of the middle 50%.


Deviation
Difference between a score and the mean.


Sum of squares (SS)
Sum of squared deviations from the mean.


Population variance
(SS/N).


Sample variance
(SS/(n-1)).


Standard deviation
Square root of variance; spread in original units.


Degrees of freedom
Number of independently free scores used in estimating sample variance; (n-1).


Unbiased estimator
Statistic that equals the target population parameter on average across repeated samples.


Real limit
Boundary extending halfway between adjacent measurable values.

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
40. Common Misunderstandings

“The mode has to be a number.”
No. The mode can be a category.


“A distribution can only have one mode.”
No. It can be bimodal or multimodal.


“The median is always an observed score.”
No. It can lie between observed scores or be interpolated within an interval.


“The mean is always the best measure of center.”
No. Extreme scores can make it misleading.


“A positively skewed distribution has most scores on the right.”
No. The tail points right; most observations are concentrated more toward the lower side.


“Variance and standard deviation are the same thing.”
No. Standard deviation is the square root of variance.


“Standard deviation can be negative.”
No. Variability cannot be negative.


“Sample and population variance use the same denominator.”
No. Population variance divides by (N); sample variance divides by (n-1).


“Using (n-1) is just a strange convention.”
No. It corrects the systematic downward bias that occurs when sample variance is calculated with (n), and it corresponds to the degrees of freedom available after estimating the mean.


“If I add 10 to every score, standard deviation increases by 10.”
No. The mean shifts, but the distances between scores and their mean remain unchanged.


“If I multiply every score by 10, variance also multiplies by 10.”
No. Standard deviation multiplies by 10; variance multiplies by:
\[
10^2=100.
\]

title: Week 03 — Central Tendency, Shape, and Variability
text:
41. Tutorial Preparation
A TA should be ready to explain both procedures and why the procedures work.

“Why are there three measures of central tendency?”
Because they define “center” differently and respond differently to scale, skewness, and outliers.


“Why can’t I average group means?”
You can only do that directly when the groups contribute equally. With unequal sample sizes, use a weighted mean.


“Why does the mean move toward an outlier?”
Because every score contributes its magnitude to the total sum.


“Why does the median resist outliers?”
Because it depends primarily on ordered position rather than the magnitude of extreme values.


“Why do we square deviations?”
Because signed deviations sum to zero. Squaring prevents cancellation and produces a positive measure of spread.


“Why take the square root afterward?”
Because variance is in squared units. The square root produces standard deviation in the original units.


“Why (n-1)?”
Because estimating the sample mean consumes one degree of freedom, and dividing by (n-1) corrects the average downward bias in sample variance.


“Why does adding a constant not change SD?”
Because every score and the mean shift by exactly the same amount, so the deviations remain unchanged.
